title: CI/CD explained: from code commit to production
seoTitle: CI/CD Explained: Continuous Integration and Delivery Guide
seoDescription: Understand continuous integration, continuous delivery and deployment, pipeline stages, testing, releases and common CI/CD mistakes.
excerpt: CI/CD creates a repeatable path from a code change to tested, releasable software.
author: KitsuWire Editorial
keyTakeaways: Continuous integration merges small changes frequently and validates them automatically.
Continuous delivery keeps software releasable; continuous deployment can automatically release every qualifying change.
A pipeline is only as trustworthy as its tests, security, environment consistency and rollback strategy.
body: A software release can involve compilation, tests, security checks, packaging, infrastructure and deployment. Performing those steps manually makes results depend on memory and individual machines.
CI/CD turns the path from commit to release into an automated, observable process.

sections.heading: Continuous integration
paragraphs: Continuous integration encourages developers to integrate changes frequently instead of maintaining long-lived divergent branches. Each change triggers automated validation such as compilation, unit tests and static analysis.
The objective is fast feedback. A defect discovered minutes after a commit is generally easier to diagnose than one discovered after weeks of accumulated changes.

sections.heading: Continuous delivery vs continuous deployment
paragraphs: Continuous delivery means the main branch is kept in a releasable state and deployment is automated enough that a release can be triggered reliably. A human approval may still decide when production changes occur.
Continuous deployment goes further by automatically deploying changes that satisfy the pipeline's controls. The terms are related but should not be treated as identical.

sections.heading: Typical pipeline stages
paragraphs: A pipeline may install dependencies, build an artifact, run tests, scan dependencies, build a container image, publish it to a registry, deploy to an environment and run post-deployment checks.
The artifact promoted toward production should ideally be the same tested artifact rather than being rebuilt differently at every stage.

sections.heading: Secrets and pipeline security
paragraphs: Pipelines often hold powerful credentials for registries, clouds and production environments. Secrets should be stored in protected secret systems rather than committed to source control or printed in logs.
Modern designs increasingly use short-lived identity federation instead of long-lived static cloud keys. Pipeline permissions should follow least privilege.

sections.heading: Deployment strategies
paragraphs: Rolling deployments gradually replace instances. Blue-green deployments maintain old and new environments and switch traffic. Canary releases expose a new version to a limited audience before wider rollout.
No strategy removes the need for monitoring. Teams need signals that tell them whether the new version is healthy and a tested way to stop or reverse a bad release.

sections.heading: Common CI/CD mistakes
paragraphs: A pipeline that takes an hour provides slow feedback and encourages developers to bypass it. Flaky tests destroy trust because failures stop meaning something. Excessive manual gates can turn automation back into a ticket process.
The best pipelines optimize for trustworthy feedback and safe flow rather than maximizing the number of tools involved.

faq.question: What does CI/CD stand for?
faq.answer: CI means continuous integration. CD commonly refers to continuous delivery or continuous deployment depending on the workflow.

faq.question: Does CI/CD require containers?
faq.answer: No. Pipelines can build and deploy software to VMs, serverless services, mobile stores, Kubernetes and many other targets.

faq.question: Can CI/CD deploy directly to production?
faq.answer: Yes, in a continuous-deployment model, but only when automated quality, security, observability and rollback controls make that risk acceptable.
